optInNurture.goal: Convert an explicitly opted-in lead into a booked analytics audit.
optInNurture.narrativeArc: Diagnose reporting friction, quantify the operating cost, explain the team model, show relevant use cases, remove risk, and invite a practical first conversation.

subjectOptions: Your analytics audit: where to start
The first reporting problem to fix
One question before we talk data
emails.previewText: Start with the decision that is hardest to make today.
emails.purpose: Set expectations and help the lead identify the highest-value reporting problem.
emails.body:
Hi {{ contact.FNAME }},

Thanks for requesting a KPIBoard analytics audit.

The best place to start is not a dashboard. It is a decision your team currently makes too slowly, with too much manual work, or with numbers nobody fully trusts.

Before our conversation, choose one recurring question that creates the most friction. It might be:

• Which products and channels are actually profitable?
• Where are we likely to run out of stock?
• Why do Finance and Marketing report different revenue?
• Which customers are worth acquiring again?

Reply with that one question. We will use it to make the audit specific and useful.

Best,
KPIBoard

subjectOptions: Choose the use case, not the dashboard
Four places analytics usually pays back
Where should a BI team start?
emails.previewText: Start where uncertainty creates a measurable operating cost.
emails.purpose: Help leads select a first use case by decision value.
emails.body:
Hi {{ contact.FNAME }},

A first analytics project should be narrow enough to ship and important enough to change a decision.

Four useful starting points are:

1. Profitability — connect revenue, discounts, fees, refunds, COGS, and ad spend.
2. Inventory — combine demand, stock, lead times, and purchasing risk.
3. Growth efficiency — connect acquisition cost to contribution margin and customer value.
4. Executive control — align revenue, cash, pipeline, service, and targets.

The right choice is the one where a better answer changes what your team does next week.

Reply with 1, 2, 3, or 4 and we will send you the questions we use to scope it.
emails.condition: Send unless the lead replied, unsubscribed, or booked.

subjectOptions: What the first four weeks look like
A practical path from systems to signal
emails.previewText: No six-month black box—just visible stages and review points.
emails.purpose: Reduce implementation anxiety by showing a staged delivery process.
emails.body:
Hi {{ contact.FNAME }},

Analytics projects feel risky when the plan is vague and value appears only at the end.

We use visible stages instead:

Week 1: clarify the decision, KPIs, owners, sources, and architecture.
Week 2: connect and transform the required data.
Week 3: build and validate the semantic model.
Week 4+: ship the first decision view, automate it, and improve it in review cycles.

Timing depends on access and data quality, so we do not promise an artificial universal deadline. We do promise a clear priority, visible progress, and early feedback.

If you want, we can map the first stage before you commit to a larger build.

emails.previewText: A simple yes, later, or no is enough.
emails.purpose: Create a respectful final decision point and clean the active nurture pool.
emails.body:
Hi {{ contact.FNAME }},

I have sent a few ideas about turning scattered reporting into a trusted decision system.

Should we keep the conversation open?

Reply with:

• Yes — analytics is a current priority.
• Later — check back in a future quarter.
• No — close the loop.

If it is a current priority, we can use a short audit to identify the first decision, required systems, and practical next step.

Either way, a one-word reply is helpful.

Best,
KPIBoard

sequences.audience: E-commerce founders, CFOs, COOs, and heads of growth at multi-channel brands.

subjects: Shopify, ads, ERP—and one profit number
A question about your margin reporting
emails.body:
Hi,

Growing commerce teams often have the same reporting pattern: Shopify shows sales, Meta and Google show attribution, the ERP shows stock, and Finance has the final margin spreadsheet.

Each system can be correct on its own while leadership still lacks one trusted profit view.

KPIBoard connects those systems into a governed model so teams can see contribution margin, channel economics, and inventory risk without rebuilding reports every week.

Is unified profitability reporting a current priority?

If this is not relevant, reply “no” and I will close the loop.

subjects: The ROAS number Finance cannot use
emails.body:
Hi,

A campaign can look profitable in an ad platform and still lose money after discounts, returns, payment fees, shipping, and product cost.

That gap is why we combine acquisition data with order and finance data—not just another marketing dashboard.

The result is a view of which channels, campaigns, products, and cohorts create real contribution.

Worth comparing this with how your team calculates profitability today?

If you prefer no follow-up, reply “no.”

subjects: Stockouts rarely start in the warehouse
Demand, lead time, and cash in one view
emails.body:
Hi,

Inventory problems are usually visible in several places before they become urgent: changing demand, supplier lead time, purchase orders, campaign plans, and current stock.

The difficulty is bringing those signals together early enough to act.

KPIBoard builds inventory decision models that surface stockout exposure, overstock, sell-through, and working-capital pressure in one operating view.

Would an inventory-risk audit be useful?

Reply “no” if I should stop here.
